name: Tishman

profile.address: 165 Halsey / Equinix NY1 / Databank EWR1, 165, Halsey Street, Teachers Village, The Ironbound, Newark, Essex County, New Jersey, 07102
profile.reading:
The fourteen story building at 165 Halsey Street in downtown Newark, New Jersey, is one of the more storied carrier hotel and data center properties in the New York City metropolitan area, even though it sits across the Hudson in New Jersey rather than in Manhattan itself. It was built in 1912 as a department store for L. Bamberger and Company, one of the country's largest retailers in the early twentieth century, and was expanded twice before 1929 to reach roughly 1.2 million square feet. Bamberger's parent, Macy's, closed the store in 1992, and the building sat vacant for several years afterward. Developer Samuel Jemal recognized that the structure's heavy floor loading and large open floor plates, features originally meant to support a department store's merchandise and foot traffic, were also well suited to telecommunications equipment and raised access flooring, and conversion of the building into carrier and data center space began in 1996.

Today the building houses multiple, separately branded operations rather than a single tenant. Equinix operates a facility it calls NY1 on part of the building, describing an eighth floor site of roughly 21,775 square feet built around 2N power redundancy, 120 and 208 volt power distribution, and diesel generator backup rated for 30 hours or more at full load. DataBank operates a separate facility it calls EWR1, describing roughly 34,360 square feet of IT space, 1.7 megawatts of critical IT load, and 21 carriers present on site. Other long documented tenants of the broader building include Level 3 Communications, Verizon Business, CenturyLink, BT Americas, Telecom Italia Sparkle, and Zayo Group, and the building is understood to be a landing point for the Apollo transatlantic submarine cable system as well as a host to multiple internet exchange points, all consistent with its role as one of the New York area's significant interconnection hubs outside Manhattan. Some commercial data center directories associate an entity called Tishman with the building's property or facilities management, but that link has not been corroborated in primary sources and should be treated as an unverified lead rather than a confirmed fact. What is well established is that this is a large, multi tenant, historically significant conversion of early twentieth century retail space into modern telecommunications infrastructure, still expanding its carrier and colocation footprint more than a century after it first opened as a store.

Built in 1912 as a Bamberger's department store and expanded twice by 1929, the fourteen story, 1.2 million square foot building sat vacant after Macy's closed the store in 1992 until developer Samuel Jemal recognized its sturdy floor loading and large open floor plates as well suited to telecommunications and data center use, beginning conversion in 1996. Documented tenants include Equinix, which operates its NY1 facility there and is separately profiled in this registry Equinix facility cluster, along with Level 3 Communications, Verizon Business, CenturyLink, BT Americas, Telecom Italia Sparkle, and Zayo Group; the building is also a landing point for the Apollo transatlantic submarine cable system and hosts multiple internet exchange points. Commercial data center directories including Baxtel, Inflect, and Cloudscene list an entity called Tishman Real Estate Services as associated with the building address, consistent with a property or facilities management role, but this was not corroborated in Wikipedia, AECOM own project page, or other primary sources, and is treated as an unverified directory level lead. The well documented Tishman corporate family split in 1976 into Tishman Speyer, Tishman Hotel and Realty LP, and a construction division later sold to AECOM in 2010, now AECOM Tishman; no source ties any of those named entities specifically to this address. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading:
This operator record exists because of a single map edit, and the company it names has no established role at the building in question. The facility row is an OpenStreetMap way covering 165 Halsey Street in Newark, New Jersey. That polygon was drawn on 22 December 2015 carrying nothing but a building tag. On 6 May 2025 one contributor added, in a single edit, the name 165 Halsey slash Equinix NY1 slash Databank EWR1, a telecom equals data_center tag, the street address, and an operator tag reading Tishman. Every attribute this registry holds for the operator called Tishman descends from that one free text field, which is why the record carries no headquarters, no website and no corroborating detail.

The municipal record does not support it. The New Jersey MOD-IV composite entry for the parcel, PAMS PIN 0714_61_33 in Newark City, Essex County, covering block 61 lot 33 with an additional lot 45, gives the property location as 109 to 135 Market Street, a site of 1.64 acres, property class 4A, and a building description of 16SST for a sixteen storey structure, with a year of construction recorded as 1900. Land is assessed at 24,207,500 dollars and improvements at 72,792,500 dollars for a net taxable value of 97,000,000 dollars, with prior year tax of 3,688,910 dollars. The deed of record dates from 1997 at a stated price of one dollar, consistent with the period when the vacant department store was being converted. The owner mailing address on the tax roll is on West 34th Street in Manhattan. No Tishman entity appears anywhere in it.

The building itself is entirely genuine and is one of the most significant carrier hotels in the New York metropolitan area, the former Bamberger's department store converted to telecommunications and data centre use from the mid 1990s and now housing Equinix NY1 among other tenants. The plausible route by which the Tishman name became attached is construction rather than operation. AECOM lists 165 Halsey Street among its data centre projects, and AECOM Tishman is the successor to the construction arm of the old Tishman Realty and Construction business, which liquidated in 1976 and split into Tishman Speyer, Tishman Hotel and Realty, and a construction division sold to AECOM in 2010.

That is the failure worth recording. A construction manager credited on a project, or any other party loosely associated with a building, can end up in an operator tag, and a registry that groups facilities by that string without review will mint a data centre operator that does not exist. There is no company operating data centres under the name Tishman, no capacity figure of any kind should be attached to this record, and the correct disposition is to reassign the building to the operators actually present in it and retire this operator entry.
